content: 1. Influenza vaccination has been shown to be 70% effective in preventing hospitalizations due to pneumonia and influenza among the general population. 2. Among elderly individuals residing in nursing homes, the influenza vaccine is particularly effective in preventing severe illness, secondary complications, and deaths. 3. In this population, the vaccine demonstrates 50%-60% effectiveness in preventing influenza-related hospitalizations or pneumonia and up to 80% effectiveness in preventing influenza-related deaths. However, its effectiveness in preventing influenza illness itself often ranges between 30% and 40%. 4. The immunogenicity of the approved live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) has been evaluated in multiple studies, including approximately 100 children aged 5-17 years and 300 adults aged 18-49 years. 5. LAIV virus strains primarily replicate in the epithelial cells of the nasopharynx. 6. The protective mechanisms induced by LAIV vaccination are not fully understood but appear to involve both serum and nasal secretory antibodies. 7. 8. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 1,602 healthy children aged 15-71 months assessed the efficacy of trivalent LAIV against culture-confirmed influenza over two seasons. 9. In the first season, when the vaccine and circulating virus strains were well-matched, the efficacy of two doses of LAIV was 93%. 10. In the second season, when the A(H3N2) component of the vaccine was not well-matched to circulating strains, the overall efficacy was 86%. 11. Over the two-season study, the vaccine was 92% effective in preventing culture-confirmed influenza. 12. Additional findings included a 27% reduction in febrile otitis media and a 28% reduction in otitis media requiring concurrent antibiotic use. 13. Receipt of LAIV also resulted in 21% fewer febrile illnesses. 14. A review of LAIV effectiveness in children aged 18 months to 18 years found an 18% reduction in medically attended acute respiratory illness (MAARI), with higher efficacy levels of 92% against influenza A(H1N1) and 66% against an influenza B drift variant. 15. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial among 4,561 healthy working adults aged 18-64 years assessed multiple endpoints, including reductions in self-reported respiratory tract illness, absenteeism, healthcare visits, and medication use during peak and total influenza outbreak periods. 16. During the 1997-98 influenza season, when the vaccine and circulating A(H3N2) strains were not well-matched, no difference in febrile illnesses was observed between LAIV and placebo recipients during peak outbreak periods. 17. However, vaccination was associated with a 19% reduction in severe febrile illnesses and a 24% reduction in febrile upper respiratory tract illnesses. 18. Vaccination also resulted in fewer days of illness, fewer days of work lost, fewer healthcare-provider visits, and reduced use of prescription antibiotics and over-the-counter medications. 19. Among a subset of 3,637 healthy adults aged 18-49 years, LAIV recipients experienced 26% fewer febrile upper respiratory illness episodes, 27% fewer lost workdays due to febrile upper respiratory illness, and 18%-37% fewer healthcare-provider visits for febrile illness compared to placebo recipients. 20. Days of antibiotic use were reduced by 41%-45% in this age group. 21. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge study among 92 healthy adults aged 18-41 years assessed the efficacy of both LAIV and inactivated influenza vaccine. 22. The overall efficacy of LAIV and inactivated influenza vaccine in preventing laboratory-documented influenza from all three influenza strains combined was 85% and 71%, respectively, based on experimental challenge with viruses to which participants were susceptible before vaccination. 23. The difference in efficacy between the two vaccines was not statistically significant. 24. Influenza vaccination has been shown to reduce both healthcare costs and productivity losses associated with influenza illness. 25. Studies in the United States have reported substantial reductions in hospitalizations, deaths, and overall societal cost savings among individuals aged >65 years following influenza vaccination. 26. Among adults aged <65 years, vaccination has been shown to reduce both direct medical costs and indirect costs from work absenteeism. 27. Reductions of 13%-44% in healthcare-provider visits, 18%-45% in lost workdays, 18%-28% in days working with reduced effectiveness, and 25% in antibiotic use for influenza-associated illnesses have been reported. 28. One cost-effectiveness analysis estimated a cost of approximately $60-$4,000 per illness averted among healthy individuals aged 18-64 years, depending on vaccination cost, influenza attack rate, and vaccine effectiveness against influenza-like illness. 29. Another cost-benefit study estimated average annual savings of $13.66 per vaccinated person, with 78% of all costs prevented attributed to productivity losses from influenza illness. 30. Economic studies specifically evaluating the cost-effectiveness of vaccinating individuals aged 50-64 years are not available, and studies examining the economics of routinely vaccinating children with trivalent inactivated vaccine (TIV) or LAIV are limited. 31. In a study of inactivated vaccine across all age groups, cost utility (cost per year of healthy life gained) improved with increasing age and among those with chronic medical conditions. 32. Among individuals aged >65 years, vaccination resulted in net savings per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained, whereas among younger age groups, vaccination resulted in costs of $23-$256 per QALY. 33. Less than half of respondents in a survey on public perception of the value of preventing influenza morbidity reported that they would trade any time from their own life to prevent a case of uncomplicated influenza in a hypothetical child. 34. When asked about their willingness to pay to prevent a hypothetical child from having an uncomplicated case of influenza, the median willingness-to-pay amount was $100 for a 14-year-old child and $175 for a 1-year-old child. 35. One of the national health objectives for 2010 was to achieve an influenza vaccination coverage level of 90% for individuals aged >65 years. 36. Among individuals aged >65 years, influenza vaccination levels increased from 33% in 1989 to 66% in 1999, surpassing the Healthy People 2000 objective of 60%. 37. Vaccination coverage in this group reached the highest recorded level of 68% during the 1999-2000 influenza season. 38. This estimate was based on the percentage of adults reporting influenza vaccination during the previous 12 months in the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). 39.
